name: Évora
tagline: A walled Alentejo city built directly around a 2,000-year-old Roman temple, with a genuinely unsettling chapel walled entirely in human bones.
highlight: The Roman Temple of Évora at dusk, its Corinthian columns floodlit against the sky at the heart of a city that's kept building around them for two millennia.
shortDescription: A UNESCO-listed walled city in Portugal's Alentejo region, its Roman temple and bone-walled chapel among the country's most striking historic sights.
metaDescription: An Évora travel guide: the Roman Temple, the Chapel of Bones, Alentejo wine, when to go and a practical two-day itinerary.
knownFor: The Roman Temple, the Chapel of Bones, Alentejo wine country
goodFor: History, archaeology, wine, a quieter alternative to the coast

image.alt: The Roman Temple of Évora, its ancient columns standing at the heart of the city

intro: Évora is the Alentejo region's historic capital, a genuinely well-preserved walled city whose layered history — Roman, Moorish, medieval — remains visible in a way few Portuguese cities can match, all recognised with UNESCO World Heritage status for the old town as a whole.

The city's most striking sight is genuinely its most literal: a 2nd-century Roman temple stands nearly intact at the heart of the old town, its Corinthian columns surviving centuries of reuse as a slaughterhouse and fortress before its true nature was rediscovered.

That ancient history sits alongside the genuinely unsettling Chapel of Bones, its interior walls and columns built from the skulls and bones of thousands of monks and locals, and a surrounding Alentejo countryside of cork oak plains and increasingly respected wine estates that reward slowing down beyond the city walls.

whyVisit.intro: Évora's case is that no other Portuguese city holds this much visible ancient history within one genuinely walkable walled centre.

points.title: The Roman Temple is genuinely remarkable
points.text: Standing nearly intact at the city's heart, one of the best-preserved Roman temples on the Iberian Peninsula.

points.title: The Chapel of Bones is genuinely unforgettable
points.text: An interior built entirely from human bones, unlike anything else on a typical Portugal itinerary.

points.title: The old town is genuinely dense with layered history
points.text: Roman, Moorish and medieval architecture sit within a compact, UNESCO-listed walled centre.

points.title: The Alentejo wine country is genuinely excellent
points.text: Increasingly respected wine estates surround the city, considerably less crowded than the Douro Valley.

points.title: It's genuinely much quieter than Lisbon or Porto
points.text: A relaxed, low-key pace with a fraction of the coastal cities' visitor numbers.

attractionsIntro: Évora's essential sights, spanning its Roman, medieval and religious layers of history.

attractions.name: Roman Temple of Évora

image.alt: The Roman Temple of Évora, its ancient columns standing at the heart of the city

attractions.text: A 2nd-century temple, likely dedicated to the cult of Emperor Augustus, its Corinthian columns genuinely among the best preserved Roman remains anywhere in Portugal.
attractions.tip: Visit at dusk when the temple is floodlit — the columns take on a genuinely striking presence against the darkening sky.

attractions.name: Chapel of Bones (Capela dos Ossos)
attractions.text: A genuinely macabre 16th-century chapel, its walls and columns built from the bones and skulls of thousands of monks and locals, intended as a meditation on mortality.
attractions.tip: The chapel's Latin inscription at the entrance, translating roughly to 'we bones, here, await yours,' genuinely sets the tone.

attractions.name: Évora Cathedral (Sé de Évora)
attractions.text: A genuinely imposing granite Gothic cathedral, its rooftop terrace offering sweeping views over the old town's rooftops.
attractions.tip: Climb to the cathedral's rooftop terrace for genuinely one of the best views in the city.

attractions.name: University of Évora
attractions.text: A genuinely historic university, its main courtyard lined with azulejo-tiled classrooms still in active academic use.
attractions.tip: Free to wander the main courtyard and admire the tilework, even without a formal tour.

attractions.name: Praça do Giraldo
attractions.text: Évora's central square, genuinely the social heart of the city, ringed by cafés and arcaded buildings.
attractions.tip: A good spot to simply sit with a coffee and watch the city's genuinely unhurried daily rhythm.

attractions.name: The city walls and aqueduct
attractions.text: Évora's medieval walls and the 16th-century Água de Prata aqueduct, genuinely worth a walk for a different perspective on the city's layered architecture.
attractions.tip: Parts of the aqueduct have genuinely been built directly into, with houses incorporated along its arches.

thingsToDoIntro: Beyond the Roman and religious sights, Évora rewards the surrounding Alentejo countryside and its wine culture.

thingsToDo.title: Taste Alentejo wine at a local estate
thingsToDo.text: The Alentejo has become genuinely one of Portugal's most respected wine regions, its estates producing excellent reds from the plains surrounding Évora.
thingsToDo.tip: Several wine estates near Évora offer genuinely worthwhile tours combining tastings with the region's cork oak landscape.

thingsToDo.title: Explore the cork oak countryside
thingsToDo.text: The Alentejo produces a genuinely significant share of the world's cork, its distinctive oak groves a defining feature of the landscape around Évora.
thingsToDo.tip: A countryside drive or guided tour explains the genuinely fascinating, sustainable cork harvesting process.

thingsToDo.title: Visit the Cromlech of the Almendres
thingsToDo.text: A genuinely significant prehistoric stone circle predating Stonehenge, a short drive from Évora and considerably less visited than its British counterpart.
thingsToDo.tip: A rental car or organised tour is genuinely necessary — public transport doesn't reach the site well.

thingsToDo.title: Wander Évora's old town streets
thingsToDo.text: The genuinely compact walled centre rewards slow, unhurried wandering beyond the headline sights.
thingsToDo.tip: Évora's whitewashed houses with yellow trim are a genuinely distinctive Alentejo architectural style worth noticing.

thingsToDo.title: Visit a nearby Alentejo village
thingsToDo.text: Villages like Monsaraz, a genuinely picturesque hilltop settlement, offer a worthwhile day trip into the wider Alentejo countryside.
thingsToDo.tip: Monsaraz overlooks the Alqueva reservoir, Europe's largest artificial lake, genuinely worth the detour for the view alone.

foodIntro: Évora sits at the heart of Alentejo cuisine, genuinely distinct from the rest of Portugal for its bread-based dishes and excellent wine.

foods.name: Açorda alentejana
foods.text: A genuinely simple, satisfying bread soup flavoured with garlic, coriander and olive oil, often topped with a poached egg, an Alentejo staple.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional restaurants throughout Évora's old town.

foods.name: Migas
foods.text: Fried breadcrumbs typically served alongside pork, a genuinely hearty Alentejo dish reflecting the region's tradition of using every part of the bread.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional Alentejo restaurants throughout the city.

foods.name: Alentejo wine
foods.text: Increasingly respected reds from the plains surrounding Évora, genuinely excellent and considerably less internationally known than Douro wines.
foods.whereToTry: Wine estates around Évora, or wine bars throughout the old town.

foods.name: Porco preto (black Iberian pork)
foods.text: Pork from free-range black pigs fed partly on acorns from the region's cork and holm oak forests, genuinely one of the Alentejo's finest products.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional restaurants throughout Évora, often served simply grilled.

foods.name: Queijo Serpa cheese
foods.text: A genuinely distinctive sheep's milk cheese from the wider Alentejo region, with a soft, creamy texture and protected geographic status.
foods.whereToTry: Local markets and traditional restaurants throughout Évora.

accommodation.intro: Évora's walled old town offers a genuinely convenient, compact base for most visitors.

areas.name: Inside the city walls
areas.bestFor: Walking to the Roman Temple and main sights
areas.text: The most central, historic base, putting Évora's main attractions within easy walking distance.

areas.name: A rural quinta near Évora
areas.text: Several converted country estates near the city offer a genuinely peaceful, rural alternative to staying in town.

gettingThere.intro: Évora is an easy train or bus trip from Lisbon, or a short drive through the Alentejo countryside.

options.text: Direct trains from [[lisbon|Lisbon]] reach Évora in about 1.5 hours.
options.detail: A genuinely comfortable, straightforward connection with no changes required.

options.text: Regular buses offer a comparable journey time to the train, often at a lower price.
options.detail: A reasonable alternative if train timings don't suit your schedule.

options.text: Offers the flexibility to explore the wider Alentejo countryside, including the Cromlech of the Almendres and nearby villages.
options.detail: Genuinely worthwhile if combining Évora with wine estates or countryside villages beyond the city itself.

gettingAround.intro: Évora's walled old town is genuinely compact and entirely walkable.

options.text: The Roman Temple, cathedral and Chapel of Bones all sit within a genuinely compact, walkable historic centre.
options.detail: The old town's flat layout within the walls makes walking considerably easier than in Lisbon or Porto.

options.text: Necessary for reaching the Cromlech of the Almendres, wine estates and nearby villages like Monsaraz.
options.detail: Public transport to these outlying sites is genuinely limited.

bestTime.headline: April–June and September–October, for mild weather in a genuinely hot inland region
bestTime.summary: Évora's inland Alentejo location makes it genuinely hotter in summer than Portugal's coastal cities, favouring spring and autumn visits.

seasons.text: Mild, increasingly warm weather, ideal for walking the old town and countryside before summer's inland heat.
Genuinely intense heat, often exceeding 35°C, being considerably further inland than the coast.
Comfortable temperatures and the wine harvest in the surrounding countryside.
Mild and genuinely quiet, with the Alentejo countryside at its greenest after autumn rains.

bestTime.avoid: Midday hours outdoors in July and August, when the Alentejo's inland heat genuinely exceeds coastal Portugal by a significant margin.

itinerary.intro: The Roman Temple and Chapel of Bones first, then the surrounding Alentejo countryside.

days.title: The old town
days.morning: The Roman Temple and Évora Cathedral.
days.afternoon: The Chapel of Bones and University of Évora.

days.title: Alentejo wine and countryside
days.summary: The region beyond the city walls.
days.afternoon: A wine estate tour and tasting.

tipsIntro: Practical notes on booking, timing and transport that make a real difference to an Évora trip.
tips: Visit the Roman Temple at dusk when it's floodlit for a genuinely striking view.
Rent a car if you want to visit the Cromlech of the Almendres or nearby villages like Monsaraz.
Pack for genuine inland heat in summer — Évora runs considerably hotter than coastal Lisbon or Porto.
Book a wine estate tour ahead, particularly during the autumn harvest season.
Wear comfortable shoes for the old town's cobblestones, though the terrain itself is genuinely flatter than Lisbon or Porto.
Combine Évora with a countryside day trip if you have time — the wider Alentejo genuinely rewards it.

faq.q: Is Évora worth a day trip from Lisbon?
faq.a: It's possible as a day trip, but an overnight stay is genuinely better — the Roman Temple lit at dusk and the surrounding wine country reward more time than a rushed single day allows.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Évora?
faq.a: Two days covers the old town's Roman and religious sights comfortably, with a countryside day for wine tasting or the Cromlech of the Almendres a worthwhile addition.

faq.q: What is the Chapel of Bones?
faq.a: A 16th-century chapel whose interior walls and columns are built from the bones and skulls of thousands of monks and locals, intended as a meditation on mortality — genuinely one of Portugal's most unusual sights.
No, genuinely one of Portugal's more affordable regions — mid-range travel runs roughly €65–120 per person per day, noticeably below Lisbon and comparable to Porto.

faq.q: What is the best time of year to visit?
faq.a: April to June and September to October offer the most comfortable weather. Évora's inland Alentejo location runs genuinely hotter than coastal Portugal in July and August.
